propositions.text: The Applicant is an Iranian citizen, filmmaker and human rights activist who came to Canada in 2004 and was granted refugee protection in 2005.
propositions.quote: The Applicant is an Iranian citizen, filmmaker and human rights activist, who came to Canada in 2004. She was granted refugee protection in 2005 based on her activities as a student activist in Iran, her gender and her affiliation to her mother and sister (who are both politically active and outspoken).

propositions.text: The Applicant obtained permanent resident status in 2008 and travelled back to Iran 16 times using an Iranian passport renewed or obtained after permanent resident status.
propositions.quote: The Applicant obtained permanent resident status in 2008. Since then, she has travelled back to Iran 16 times, as well as to other countries, using an Iranian passport renewed or obtained after she obtained her permanent resident status.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant is an Iranian filmmaker and activist granted refugee protection in 2005, became permanent resident in 2008, and travelled to Iran 16 times using an Iranian passport.

propositions.text: In November 2019, the Minister brought a cessation application under section 108 IRPA, and the RPD granted it on March 13, 2023, ending the Applicant's refugee protection and permanent resident status.
propositions.quote: In November 2019, the Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness [Minister] brought an application for cessation of her refugee status pursuant to section 108 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA]. On March 13, 2023, the Refugee Protection Division [RPD] of the Immigration and Refugee Board granted the cessation application. As a result, the Applicant’s claim for refugee protection was rejected and she lost her permanent resident status.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Minister applied for cessation in 2019, and the RPD granted it in 2023, ending the Applicant's refugee protection and permanent resident status.

propositions.text: The Applicant challenges the RPD’s cessation decision, alleging errors in assessing her intention to reavail and actual reavailment.
propositions.quote: On this application, the Applicant challenges the RPD’s cessation decision, asserting that the RPD made numerous errors in the manner in which they assessed her intention to reavail and whether she actually reavailed.

propositions.text: The court finds the RPD’s consideration of actual reavailment unreasonable and remits the matter for redetermination by a different RPD member.
propositions.quote: Having considered the various grounds of review asserted by the Applicant, I am satisfied that the RPD’s consideration of the Applicant’s actual reavailment was unreasonable and on that basis alone, the matter should be remitted for redetermination by a different member of the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant challenges the RPD’s cessation decision for errors; the court finds the RPD’s actual reavailment assessment unreasonable and remits the matter.

propositions.text: The applicable standard of review is reasonableness, requiring a 'reasons first' approach to assess transparency, intelligibility, and justification.
propositions.quote: The parties agree, and I concur, that the applicable standard of review is reasonableness. When reviewing for reasonableness, the Court must take a “reasons first” approach and determine whether the decision under review, including both its rationale and outcome, is transparent, intelligible and justified [see Mason v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 SCC 21 at para 8].

propositions.text: A reasonable decision is internally coherent, rational, and justified in relation to facts and law constraining the decision-maker.
propositions.quote: A reasonable decision is one that is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and that is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision-maker [see Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paras 15, 85].

propositions.text: The Court intervenes only if serious shortcomings undermine justification, intelligibility, and transparency of the decision.
propositions.quote: The Court will intervene only if it is satisfied there are sufficiently serious shortcomings in the decision such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency [see Adejiji-Adele v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 418 at para 11].

paragraphs.summary: The court states the reasonableness standard requires transparent, intelligible, justified decisions and intervenes only for serious shortcomings.

propositions.text: Cessation under IRPA s.108(1)(a) depends on whether the person voluntarily reavailed themselves of their country's protection.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to paragraph 108(1)(a) of the IRPA, a cessation application turns on whether the person has voluntarily reavailed themselves of the protection of their country of nationality.

propositions.text: The reavailment test has three conjunctive elements: voluntary act, intention to reavail, and actual obtaining of protection.
propositions.quote: The test for reavailment consists of three conjunctive elements: (i) the refugee must have acted voluntarily; (ii) the refugee must have intended to reavail themselves of the protection of the country of nationality; and (iii) the refugee must have actually obtained that protection [see Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Galindo Camayo, 2022 FCA 50 at para 79].

paragraphs.summary: The court explains cessation depends on voluntary reavailment, requiring voluntary act, intention, and actual obtaining of protection.

propositions.text: There is a rebuttable presumption that refugees returning with their national passport intend to reavail themselves of that country's protection.
propositions.quote: The presumption is that refugees who return to their country of nationality, using the passport of that country, intend to reavail themselves of that country’s protection. The presumption is, however, rebuttable with sufficient evidence of compelling, fact-specific reasons [see Camayo, supra at paras 63, 65; Wu v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 FC 1071 at para 22].

paragraphs.summary: The court states a rebuttable presumption exists that refugees returning with their national passport intend to reavail themselves of that country's protection.

propositions.text: Cessation decisions have serious consequences, requiring reasons that reflect the stakes and meaningfully engage central issues and arguments.
propositions.quote: A decision to cease an individual’s refugee protection has serious and particularly harsh consequences for the affected individual. Finding that an individual has voluntarily reavailed themselves of the protection of their country of nationality will not only result in the cessation of their Convention refugee status, but also the loss of their permanent residency in Canada [see Camayo, supra at paras 50-51(a); Omer v Canada (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship), 2022 FC 1295 at para 39]. Given the significant impact of a cessation decision, the RPD’s reasons must “reflect the stakes” and thus, there is an increased duty to provide reasons that explain the decision-maker’s rationale and meaningfully engage with the central issues and arguments: [see Vavilov, supra at para 133; Camayo, supra at paras 49-51; Singh v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 1481 at para 28].

paragraphs.summary: The court explains cessation decisions have serious consequences, requiring reasons that reflect the stakes and engage central issues and arguments.

propositions.text: The case turns on whether the Applicant actually obtained protection of her country of nationality (third element of reavailment test).
propositions.quote: This case turns on the third element of the test — namely, whether the Applicant actually obtained the protection of the country of her nationality.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the case hinges on whether the Applicant actually obtained her country's protection.

propositions.text: The RPD found that by using her Iranian passport to return, the Applicant obtained Iran’s diplomatic protection and intended to reavail.
propositions.quote: The RPD determined that by returning to Iran on her Iranian passport, the Applicant obtained Iran’s protection. In its reasons, the RPD stated: [84] By applying for and using her national passport the Respondent has obtained the diplomatic protection of her country of nationality. In Cerna, the Federal Court held that when a refugee acquires a passport in order to return to his country of origin, the refugee has also obtained actual protection from that state. Protection was granted to the Respondent by Iran when she entered Iran using her national passport, and the fact that she returned to Iran on her national passport speaks to her intent to reavail.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Applicant obtained Iran’s diplomatic protection by using her Iranian passport to return, indicating intent to reavail.

propositions.text: The RPD failed to address evidence that Iranian authorities seized the Applicant’s passport in 2018, preventing her from leaving Iran.
propositions.quote: However, in reaching this conclusion, the RPD failed to grapple with the evidence put forward by the Applicant to rebut the presumption that she obtained actual diplomatic protection based on using her Iranian passport to travel to Iran. Specifically, the evidence before the RPD was that when the Applicant returned to Iran in September of 2018, the Iranian authorities seized her passport and prevented her from leaving the country due to her participation in a German documentary about Iran.

propositions.text: The Applicant was unable to leave Iran until 2020 due to passport seizure, contradicting the RPD’s finding of obtaining diplomatic protection.
propositions.quote: The Applicant was unable to secure the release of her passport until 2020, during which time she was unable to leave Iran. As this evidence directly contradicted the RPD’s finding that the Applicant had obtained the diplomatic protection of Iran, the RPD was required to address this evidence and explain why it did not amount to a denial of diplomatic protection.

propositions.text: The RPD did not engage with this evidence or the Applicant’s arguments that she did not obtain diplomatic protection.
propositions.quote: The RPD’s reasons do not engage with this evidence or the Applicant’s arguments that she did not, in fact, obtain diplomatic protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD failed to address evidence that the Applicant’s passport was seized in 2018, contradicting the finding she obtained diplomatic protection.

propositions.text: The passport seizure occurred on only one of 16 trips, and the RPD made a global finding rather than trip-by-trip assessment.
propositions.quote: I am mindful that the seizure of the Applicant’s passport by the Iranian authorities occurred in relation to only one of her 16 trips to Iran and, as argued by the Respondent at the hearing, “it only takes one” trip to Iran to reavail. However, the Minister advanced all 16 trips in support of their cessation application and the RPD chose to make a global finding in relation to each element of the test, rather assessing reavailment on a trip-by-trip basis.

propositions.text: Whether the 2018 passport seizure affects reavailment on other trips is for redetermination.
propositions.quote: Whether or not the seizure of her passport in 2018 is relevant to the assessment of whether the Applicant actually obtained the diplomatic protection of Iran on her 15 other trips will be a matter for consideration on the redetermination of the Minister’s application.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the passport seizure was on one trip; the RPD made a global finding; relevance to other trips is for redetermination.

propositions.text: The RPD’s assessment of actual reavailment was unreasonable, so the decision is set aside and remitted for redetermination by a different member.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, I find that the RPD’s assessment of the third element of the reavailment test was unreasonable. As such, the RPD’s decision shall be set aside and the Minister’s cessation application shall be remitted to the RPD for redetermination by a different member.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD’s assessment unreasonable, sets aside the decision, and remits the matter for redetermination by a different member.

propositions.text: The judicial review application is granted, the RPD decision is set aside, and the matter is remitted for redetermination by a different member.
propositions.quote: JUDGMENT in IMM-3964-23 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: The application for judicial review is granted, the decision of the Refugee Protection Division dated March 13, 2023 is hereby set aside and the matter shall be remitted to the Refugee Protection Division for redetermination by a different member.

propositions.text: No question for certification is proposed or arises.
propositions.quote: The parties propose no question for certification and I agree that none arises.

paragraphs.summary: The court grants judicial review, sets aside the RPD decision, remits for redetermination, and finds no question for certification.
